section.title: Love as Strong as Death
section.sectionRationale: This is the great climax and key of the whole Song. As the couple comes up from the wilderness, the bride speaks the poem's central truth: set me as a seal over your heart, for love is as strong as death, its flame the fiercest of all, and no waters can quench it and no wealth can buy it. The closing verses gather up the bride's integrity, the worthlessness of love that is bought, and the final call, come away, my beloved.
section.thesis: Love is as strong as death and cannot be quenched or bought; the bride asks to be sealed on her beloved's heart, and the Song closes with her integrity honored and the final invitation, come away, my beloved.
section.frameNote: Three movements: coming up from the wilderness, and the Song's crowning word, set me as a seal, for love is as strong as death and unquenchable and unpurchasable; the bride's integrity as a wall and the worthlessness of Solomon's bought vineyard beside her own freely given love; and the closing exchange, let me hear your voice, and, come away, my beloved.

verses.text: Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? I roused you under the apple tree; there your mother conceived you; there she travailed and brought you forth.

Set me as a {{chotam|seal}} over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For {{ahavah|love}} is as strong as death, its {{qinah|jealousy}} as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all.
Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned.

units.label: The bride's integrity and the unbought vineyard
units.note: a wall, her own to give

verses.text: We have a little sister, and her breasts are not yet grown. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?
If she is a wall, we will build a tower of silver upon her. If she is a door, we will enclose her with panels of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace.
Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon. He leased it to the tenants. For its fruit, each was to bring a thousand shekels of silver.
But my own vineyard is mine to give; the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon, and two hundred are for those who tend its fruit.
You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it!
Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.

chotam.gloss: Seal, signet. A seal marked ownership and was worn close, over the heart or on the arm. The bride asks to be set as a seal on her beloved, love as belonging, permanence, and pledge, held always near.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The word that crowns the whole Song here: love is as strong as death, unquenchable by any flood, unpurchasable by any wealth. This is the covenant love the Song has celebrated, now named in its full strength.

qinah.gloss: Jealousy, ardent zeal. Not petty envy but the fierce, exclusive devotion that will not share the beloved; as unrelenting as the grave, the same zeal Scripture ascribes to God for His people.

basic.context: This is the summit of the whole Song, its key verse and crowning truth. As the couple comes up from the wilderness, leaning together, the bride speaks the words the whole book has been moving toward: set me as a seal over your heart, for love is as strong as death. Its flame is the fiercest of all; no flood can quench it and no fortune can buy it. Then the closing scene honors the bride's integrity, she is a wall, her love her own to give, not for sale like Solomon's leased vineyard, and the Song ends as it lived, with the call, come away, my beloved.
basic.hermeneutics: On the plain level this is the Song's great statement about covenant love itself: that true love is powerful, permanent, exclusive, and beyond price. It cannot be extinguished or purchased, only given. Within the whole Bible, this fierce, unquenchable, jealous love is supremely the love of God for His people, love as strong as death that met death itself at the cross, and a flame that many waters could not quench.
basic.originalLanguages: The bride asks to be a chotam, a seal, worn over the heart, love as belonging and pledge. Then comes the crowning word, ahavah, love, as strong as death, and qinah, jealousy, the fierce, exclusive zeal that will not share the beloved, as unrelenting as the grave. Its flame is the fiercest of all, unquenchable and beyond all price.
basic.typology: Love as strong as death, meeting death and not being overcome, foreshadows the love of Christ that went into death and rose again. The seal over the heart pictures the pledge of belonging, and the Spirit given as the seal of those who are Christ's. The unpurchasable love points to a salvation that cannot be bought but only received.
basic.christ: Love is as strong as death, the Song says, and at the cross that love met death itself and proved stronger, for Christ loved His people to the end and death could not hold Him. The jealous, unquenchable flame is His love that no flood of judgment could put out. And a man cannot buy this love with all his wealth; it is given, as Christ gave Himself, and received by faith, not purchased.
basic.god: God's love for His people is fierce, faithful, and jealous in the holiest sense: He will not share them with idols and will not let them go. It is as strong as death and stronger, unquenchable and beyond price. He sets His people as a seal on His heart and seals them with His Spirit as the pledge that they are His.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8:38 to 39, nothing can separate us from the love of God. 1 Corinthians 15:54 to 55, death swallowed up in victory. Ephesians 1:13 to 14, sealed with the Holy Spirit as a pledge. Exodus 34:14, the LORD whose name is Jealous.
basic.oneStory: The Song reaches its summit: love is as strong as death, unquenchable and beyond price, a seal worn over the heart. It names the covenant love the whole book has celebrated and points to its source, the love of God in Christ, which met death and overcame it, and which no waters can quench and no wealth can buy.

context.literary:
The last section of the Song is a gathering of everything that has gone before, and its shape is a careful descent from a summit. The question of verse 5, 'Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?', is the third and last time the Song asks it. At 3:6 the answer was Solomon's litter, a spectacle of smoke and soldiers; at 6:10 the answer was a woman shining like the dawn; now it is a woman simply leaning on her lover. The procession has become two people walking together, and the grandeur has been exchanged for trust.

Verses 6 and 7 are the centre of the book. They are structured as a request followed by its reason, then a double image of invincibility. The request is brief, 'Set me as a seal.' The reason is three claims about love: it is as strong as death, its zeal is as unrelenting as Sheol, and its flames are the fiercest of all. Verse 7 turns to two tests, water and money, and love passes both. The parallelism is tight, with each line pairing a power of the world, death, the grave, flood, wealth, against love and finding it stronger.

Verses 8 to 12 are a second, more playful movement. They bring in the bride's family, with her brothers' talk of a 'little sister,' and then bring in Solomon and his vineyard. The pairing of the wall and the door in verse 9 against 'I am a wall' in verse 10, and of Solomon's leased vineyard in verse 11 against 'my own vineyard' in verse 12, makes a pair of contrasts that settle who owns her love. The reader should also remember Song 1:6, where her brothers made her keeper of the vineyards and she had not kept her own. The ending of chapter 8 reverses the opening of chapter 1.

The last two verses are the briefest dialogue, in which the companions are told to listen and the bridegroom is told to come. The book that began with 'Let him kiss me' ends on an invitation, with no resolution except the invitation itself.
context.historical:
The seal of verse 6 was a personal signature. In the ancient world a seal, whether a stamp or a cylinder, was pressed into clay or wax to mark ownership and to authenticate a document, and it was worn on a cord around the neck or as a ring. When Tamar asks Judah for his seal and its cord as a pledge, Genesis 38:18, she asks for the whole of his identity. The Lord promises that Zerubbabel will be 'like My signet ring,' Haggai 2:23. So to wear a seal over the heart and on the arm is to say that the beloved is one's identity, kept near the heart and visible in the hand. Aaron likewise bore the names of the tribes 'over his heart,' Exodus 28:29.

The word picture for death and Sheol belonged to the common Hebrew understanding of an inescapable realm. Sheol is the place of the dead that is 'never satisfied,' Proverbs 27:20, and Psalm 18:4-5 speaks of the 'cords of Sheol.' To say that love is as strong as death in that world is to say something extraordinary, since nothing was thought stronger.

The vineyard of verse 11 belongs to the economy of a rich estate. Solomon leases it to tenants, each owing a thousand pieces of silver, which the BSB footnote puts at about 25 pounds of silver. Baal-hamon means something like 'owner of a crowd,' a name that fits the picture of a great estate worked by many hands. The place cannot be located with confidence. The tenant system is the same one Jesus assumes in His parable of the landowner who rented out his vineyard, Matthew 21:33.

The discussion of the 'little sister' belongs to the world in which brothers acted as guardians of a girl's honour, as they did for Dinah in Genesis 34. The family's concern is for her marriageability and her purity, and the building of silver towers or the enclosure by cedar panels pictures the rewards and restraints they would apply.
context.canonical:
Verses 6 and 7 are among the most quoted lines of the Song, and they have rich ties across the canon. The language of jealousy belongs to the way God describes Himself: 'the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God,' Exodus 34:14, and 'a consuming fire, a jealous God,' Deuteronomy 4:24. Zechariah 8:2 has Him say, 'I am jealous for Zion with great zeal,' and Joel 2:18 says that the LORD 'became jealous for His land, and He spared His people.' The Song uses the same word for the bride's own love, so that the zeal of the human lover is placed alongside the zeal of God.

The imagery of death and flood belongs to Israel's songs of rescue. Psalm 124:4-5 says that without the LORD the floods would have engulfed them, and Isaiah 43:2 promises, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.' The seal that is worn on the heart has its echo in Isaiah 49:16, 'I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands,' and in the New Testament seal of the Holy Spirit, Ephesians 1:13-14 and 2 Corinthians 1:22.

The New Testament answer to 'love is as strong as death' is Romans 8:35-39, where nothing can separate us from the love of Christ, 'neither death nor life,' and 1 Corinthians 15:54-55, where death is swallowed up in victory. The scorn for bought love finds its echoes in Isaiah 55:1, 'you without money, come,' and in 1 Peter 1:18-19, where redemption was 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold.' The vineyard imagery runs to the parable of Matthew 21:33-41.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet meant the climax to say what love is, not only what it feels like. After seven chapters of images, the claim is stated plainly: love is as strong as death. The hearers are meant to see that the love in the poem is not a passing excitement but a covenant force, a bond that death itself cannot dissolve and that no flood of trouble can put out.

He also means to say that love cannot be bought. The scene with Solomon's vineyard is the poem's final, concrete argument. The king can lease land, collect rents and own a thousand shekels' worth of produce, but what the bride gives is not for sale. She is a wall, not a door, and her love is hers to give. The first hearers, in a world where marriages were arranged and wealth could be a factor, were meant to hear that true love was a different kind of thing from a transaction.

He means the closing call to be left open. 'Come away, my beloved' is not an ending but an invitation to keep going, and it gives the book its direction. Love has a goal, and the poem leaves the reader leaning forward. A reader who has understood the passage will want to guard love's integrity, to give it freely and exclusively, and to find in it a hint of something greater than itself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the passage is description in the form of praise: love is strong, jealousy is fierce, waters cannot quench it. These are not commands, and they should not be treated as threats. The jealousy of verse 6 describes the intensity of covenant love, a love that will not share the beloved. It does not authorise controlling or possessive behaviour. The same Bible condemns the jealous rage that destroys, Proverbs 6:34, and the Song's own picture of exclusive love rests on freely given commitment, not on force.

Verses 8 and 9, the brothers' talk about what to do for the little sister, are the speech of other characters and not an instruction. They show a protective family. Whether the strategy of silver towers and cedar panels is wise is left for the reader to judge, and the bride's reply that she is already a wall shows her own maturity.

What the passage plainly teaches is that love is not for sale and must not be treated as a commodity. It also teaches that the commitment of love is to be permanent and exclusive, and that is in line with Malachi 2:14-15 and Hebrews 13:4. In the light of the whole Bible, the words about the seal can be applied to marriage vows, and, beyond that, to the way believers are sealed by the Spirit.

debates.question: Is the 'fiercest blaze' of verse 6 simply a strong flame, or a 'flame of Yah'?

views.label: A superlative: the most intense flame
views.case: The Hebrew word for 'blaze' ends in the syllable yah, which in other contexts is a short form of the divine name. Many scholars hold that here it is only an intensifier, like the English phrase 'a mighty fire,' with God's name lending the flame its highest degree. This is the reading that the BSB follows in 'the fiercest blaze of all.'

views.label: The LORD's own flame
views.case: Others take the ending as the divine name and render the phrase 'a flame of the LORD.' If so, this would be the only place in the Song where God is named, and love would be said to be kindled by Him. Fire is a frequent sign of the divine presence, as at the bush, Exodus 3:2, and Deuteronomy 4:24 calls Him 'a consuming fire.'

views.label: Both, in effect
views.case: A third approach holds that the poet leaves the ambiguity as it is, so that the strongest possible fire and the fire of God are heard together. The text does not need to settle it, because love of this kind is, in the Bible's view, from God.

debates.bearing: The grammar leaves room for the first reading, and a careful reader should not rest a doctrine on the divine name here. But even the cautious reading leads to the same place: the love praised is of such a size that it can only be described by the highest comparison available, and the Bible does not hesitate to say that its source is God, 1 John 4:7-8.

debates.question: What is the point of the wall, the door and the brothers' plan?

views.label: The brothers test her purity
views.case: If she is a wall, firm and closed, they will crown her with a silver tower. If she is a door, open to anyone, they will fasten her with cedar boards. The bride replies, 'I am a wall,' and so she has proved her integrity. This reading fits the family's role and the bride's answer.

views.label: The brothers' speech is protective but unwise
views.case: Others see the brothers' talk as a contrast to the bride's own agency: their plans are about controlling a girl, while she tells how she has already become what she is by her own choice. She is not shut up by them but chooses to be a wall.

views.label: A different set of speakers
views.case: Some assign verses 8 and 9 to the daughters of Jerusalem or to a chorus, and read the question as a general one about how to treat a young woman as she nears marriage. The text does not name the speakers.

debates.bearing: The reply of verse 10 is clear: her integrity is her own. Whoever speaks in verses 8 and 9, the passage ends with a woman who knows what she is and who gives her love freely. That is the essential point, and it matches the closing contrast with Solomon's vineyard.

study.originalLanguages:
The summit verse is built from carefully chosen words. 'Strong' in 'as strong as death' is the Hebrew az, a word for strength that holds firm against force. 'Unrelenting' translates qasheh, the word for hard or severe, which is also the root of the 'stiff-necked' people of Exodus 32:9, so that the grave's grip is pictured as a hard, unyielding grasp. Love is said to match it in hardness.

The word for jealousy, qinah, is not the petty envy of English. It is the word used of the LORD's zeal, as when Phinehas was 'zealous for My sake,' Numbers 25:11, and when the LORD says, 'I am jealous for Zion with great zeal,' Zechariah 8:2. In the Song it names an exclusive devotion, a love that will not be shared. The BSB footnote notes that it can also be rendered 'passion.'

The phrase translated 'the fiercest blaze of all' is a single Hebrew word, shalhevetyah, 'flame of Yah.' The last syllable is the short form of the LORD's name, and translators divide over whether it is a divine name or a way of saying 'mighty.' It should be handled with care. In either case, the sense of intensity is unmistakable.

The seal is worn 'over your heart' and 'upon your arm.' The first image is of a seal on a cord hung around the neck, as the cord of Genesis 38:18, and the second is of a signet on the hand or arm. Both positions are the places closest to a person's life and action, the heart and the hand. Asking to be a seal is asking to be that which marks the beloved as her own and cannot be taken from him.

Verse 7 speaks of 'mighty waters,' literally 'many waters,' a standard phrase for flood and chaos, as in Psalm 124:4-5. Love is said to be unquenchable and unsweepable. Then comes the economic test. The man who gave 'all the wealth of his house' would be scorned, and the verb is buz, to treat with contempt, the same verb that opened the passage in 8:1. In verse 1 the bride feared contempt for love freely shown. In verse 7 contempt falls on love that is bought.

The verse 10 line 'I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace' turns on sound. The Hebrew for 'peace' is shalom, which echoes both Shulammite and Solomon, in Hebrew Shelomoh. The phrase may also be read as 'one who finds peace.' The play on sound suggests that in the bridegroom's eyes she is the true shalom, the fulfilment of which Solomon's own name was only a promise. Finally, the closing call 'Come away' uses a verb that elsewhere means to flee or to hasten. In Song 2:17 the bride said 'turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle,' and the last line returns to that gazelle image with a more urgent verb. Many translations read it as 'make haste,' and that gives the book's ending the sense of urgency.

typology.type: The seal over the heart and upon the arm, Song 8:6
typology.fulfillment: The high priest bore Israel's names 'over his heart,' Exodus 28:29, and the LORD says to Zion, 'I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands,' Isaiah 49:16. In the New Testament believers are 'sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,' Ephesians 1:13-14, and Paul writes that God 'placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge,' 2 Corinthians 1:22. The escalation is that the seal is God's own Spirit and not a mere mark, and it guarantees the inheritance. The type falls short because the Song's bride asks to be sealed on the beloved's heart, while in the gospel the Lord has first set His seal on His people.

typology.type: Love as strong as death, Song 8:6
typology.fulfillment: The claim that love is as strong as death is met by the cross and the empty tomb. Paul says that God proves His love in that 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8, and that death has no dominion over Him now, Romans 6:9. The risen Lord says, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18, and Paul speaks of the One 'who has abolished death,' 2 Timothy 1:10. The type falls short because the Song says love is as strong as death, while the gospel says love was stronger: death could not keep Him, Acts 2:24.

The flood imagery is taken up in Isaiah 43:2, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you,' and in the New Testament in the assurance that no trouble, distress, danger or sword 'shall separate us from the love of Christ,' Romans 8:35-39. The type pictures a love that survives every flood of trial. It falls short because the Song speaks of a love that is human in its first sense, while the unquenchable quality is perfectly true only of the love of God in Christ.

typology.type: Solomon's vineyard and a love that cannot be bought, Song 8:11-12
typology.fulfillment: A king who owns an estate and collects rents is set against a love that is given freely. The gospel speaks the same way: the redeemed were bought 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19, and salvation is 'the gift of God, not by works,' Ephesians 2:8-9. Isaiah invites 'you without money, come,' Isaiah 55:1. Jesus speaks of 'One greater than Solomon,' Matthew 12:42. The correspondence is of themes and the vineyard of the Song is not the parable's vineyard, so the link should be held lightly.

study.christ:
The summit of the Song is also a summit on the way to Christ, though the New Testament does not quote these verses directly. The path runs along four lines that the New Testament itself supplies.

The first is the strength of love against death. In the Song, love is as strong as death and as hard as the grave. In the gospel that strength is shown. Jesus said 'Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends,' John 15:13, and John wrote that having loved His own, 'He loved them to the very end,' John 13:1. Paul says, 'God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. At the cross the claim of the Song was tested to the utmost, and the result is stated by Peter: 'it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:24. The Song says love is as strong as death. The gospel says love went into death and came out.

The second line is the unquenchable flame. Many waters could not drown it, and the waters of judgment did not. The prophets use water for the troubles of the people, and the Psalmist says that apart from the LORD the floods would have engulfed us, Psalm 124:4-5. In Christ the flood of wrath is borne, and the love of Christ is the one thing from which nothing can separate His people, Romans 8:35-39.

The third is the seal. The bride asks to be set over the heart and upon the arm. In Christ believers are on His heart, as the names of the tribes were on Aaron's, and in His hands, Isaiah 49:16, and they bear His seal in the Spirit, Ephesians 1:13-14. The Song's request becomes a promise: it is the Lord who has set His seal on His people.

The fourth is the unbought love. Solomon owns a vineyard worth a fortune, but the bride's love is not for sale. Christ has the whole world and could have commanded any price, but He gave Himself, 'who loved me and gave Himself up for me,' Galatians 2:20. 'One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42. The riches of the king are nothing before a love that is freely given, and Christ shows it in a way no Solomon could.

Finally, the closing cry. 'Come away, my beloved,' the Song ends, and the Bible ends in the same spirit: 'Come, Lord Jesus,' Revelation 22:20.

A caution holds here too. The passage does not say that the bride is Christ or that Solomon is a villain, and the details of verses 8 to 12 are not coded. The sound link is that the strength, exclusiveness and price of love in the Song are fully realised in the cross, as the New Testament says.
study.god:
This passage gives the clearest teaching on love of any in the Song, and when set beside the rest of Scripture it shows several things about God.

First, God's love is strong. The claim that love is as strong as death is, for the Bible, a statement about God more than about human beings. 'God is love,' and 'God's love was revealed among us' when He sent His Son, 1 John 4:8-10. He proved it by dying, Romans 5:8, and the God who spared not His own Son, Romans 8:32, has shown that nothing is beyond the reach of His love. The strength of it is not a matter of feeling. It is shown in what it paid.

Second, God's love is jealous in the good sense. The jealousy of verse 6 is the zeal that will not share the beloved. The LORD says, 'I am jealous for Zion with great zeal,' Zechariah 8:2, and Paul writes to the Corinthians, 'I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy,' 2 Corinthians 11:2. This is not insecurity or possessiveness in a bad sense. It is the opposite of indifference. A God who did not care whether His people turned to idols would be a God who did not love them.

Third, God's love is unquenchable. Many waters cannot put it out, and the promise of Isaiah 43:2 says, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.' The prophet Hosea hears God say, 'How could I give you up, O Ephraim?' Hosea 11:8. Even in the face of Israel's unfaithfulness, His heart is turned within Him and His compassion is stirred. The love that could not be extinguished in Hosea's day is the love that sent the Son.

Fourth, God's love is not for sale. The offer of all the wealth of a house is scorned. This corrects any thought that God's favour can be earned or bargained for. The Lord says, 'You without money, come,' Isaiah 55:1, and Paul says that salvation is 'the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast,' Ephesians 2:8-9. God did not set His affection on Israel because they were many or mighty, Deuteronomy 7:7-8. He loved because He loved.

Fifth, God is a God of covenant fidelity, and the language of sealing says it. He seals His people with His Spirit as a pledge, Ephesians 1:13-14. The promise, 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' Hosea 2:19-20, is the shape of His commitment.

For worship, the passage invites us to praise the God whose love is stronger than death, to rest in His seal, and to answer His love with the freely given love of our own, saying with the bride, 'Come.'

crossReferences.note: The bride says that her mother's sons made her keeper of the vineyards while her own vineyard was neglected. In 8:12 she says her own vineyard is hers to give. The book that opened with a vineyard she could not keep ends with one she freely offers, a reversal that frames the whole Song.

The first 'Who is this coming up from the wilderness?' described Solomon's litter surrounded by soldiers. Here the same question is asked of a woman leaning on her beloved. The show of power has given way to simple trust, and the question has found its most modest and best answer.

The LORD takes the name Jealous for Himself. The word of jealousy that the Song uses of love is the word Scripture uses of God's own zeal for His people, so that the bride's burning devotion is a small reflection of the divine fire.

Aaron bears the names of the sons of Israel over his heart whenever he enters the Holy Place, as a continual reminder. The seal over the heart in Song 8:6 matches this: those who are loved are carried near the heart in the presence of God.

Zion fears she has been forgotten, and the LORD answers that He has inscribed her on the palms of His hands. It is the divine form of the bride's request: to be kept permanently in the sight and on the person of the one who loves.

Paul lists trouble, famine, sword, death and life, and says that none of them can separate us from the love of Christ. It is the New Testament statement of what the Song says in poetry: love that cannot be quenched by any flood or ended by any death.

Paul quotes the prophets in triumph over the grave. Where the Song says love is as strong as death, Paul says that death has now lost: the love of God in Christ has not merely matched death but overcome it.

The Spirit is given as the pledge of the inheritance, and Paul calls this a sealing. The seal of the Song becomes a gift of God Himself, and the one who asked to be set as a seal is answered by the one who first sealed His people.

'You without money, come, buy.' The invitation is to those who have nothing to pay with. It matches the Song's scorn for bought love and shows that God's own offer is a gift that no wealth can purchase.

The Spirit and the bride say 'Come.' The Song's last words, 'Come away, my beloved,' find their canonical echo at the close of the Bible, where the church's longing for her Lord is voiced and answered, and the book ends on the same word.

study.oneStory:
The Song is the book of love in a Bible that begins with a garden and ends with a city, and its climax tells the reader what the whole story is about. From the beginning, God made man and woman in love and set them in a place of delight. When they fell, the Bible says that death came into the world, Romans 5:12, and death became the great enemy against which every human love finally breaks. The Song's claim that love is as strong as death is therefore a claim made against the oldest sorrow in the book. Genesis 3 states the curse, and Song 8:6 sets a flame against it.

The story of Israel gives the claim its shape. God set His love on a people who were the fewest of all, Deuteronomy 7:7-8, and He bound Himself to them with a covenant, calling Himself jealous. The prophets sing of the floods that threatened her and of the LORD who passed through the waters with her, Isaiah 43:2. Israel often tried to buy other lovers and was warned that the price of such love is shame. Hosea heard God say that His heart was turned within Him, and He would not give up, Hosea 11:8, and Isaiah heard that the LORD would not forget her, Isaiah 49:16. The love of the Song is the human mirror of that covenant love.

The story reaches its centre at the cross. There the claim that love is as strong as death is tested, and the answer is given on the third day. Christ loved His own to the end, John 13:1, and rose, so that death has lost its hold, 2 Timothy 1:10. His people are sealed by the Spirit, Ephesians 1:13-14, and nothing, not death nor life, can separate them from His love, Romans 8:38-39. What the Song asks for, a seal on the heart, is given in Him.

The story ends where the Song's last words point. 'Come away, my beloved' is the cry that closes the Bible, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' Revelation 22:20. In the new creation, death is swallowed up, 1 Corinthians 15:54, and the God who is love dwells with His people. The flame that no water could quench burns in a city in which there is no more death. The Song ends with an invitation because the story does: the lovers are still calling, and the one they call is coming.

quiz.q: What does the bride ask of her beloved in 8:6?

options.text: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm.
options.note: A seal marked ownership and pledge, worn close; she asks to be held as his own.

options.text: Set me free from any claim you have on me.
options.note: A seal is indeed a claim of belonging, but she asks him to press that claim more deeply, to hold her as his own, not to set her free from it.

options.text: Keep me at a safe distance.
options.note: The seal is worn close, over the heart, the opposite of distance.

options.text: Remember me only now and then.
options.note: A seal does keep her constantly before him, but as a permanent pledge worn close, not as an occasional thought now and then.

quiz.q: How does the Song describe the strength of love in 8:6-7?

options.text: As strong as death, an unquenchable flame that no waters can drown and no wealth can buy.
options.note: The Song's crowning statement about the power and worth of love.

options.text: As fragile as a passing mood.
options.note: Love does stir deep feeling, but the point is its strength and permanence, an unquenchable flame, not a fragile passing mood.

options.text: As something easily bought with enough money.
options.note: The passage does weigh love against wealth, but only to say that riches offered for love would be utterly scorned; love cannot be bought at any price.

options.text: As weaker than the smallest trouble.
options.note: Love here is as strong as death, not weak.

quiz.q: What does the bride mean when she says, I am a wall, in 8:10?

options.text: She has kept her integrity, and her love is her own to give.
options.note: The wall pictures chastity and integrity, contrasted with a door easily entered.

options.text: She is cold and closed off to all love.
options.note: The wall does speak of being guarded, but not cold or closed to all love; she has kept her integrity and freely gives her love to her beloved.

options.text: She has been bought like a leased vineyard.
options.note: The passage does set her beside Solomon's leased vineyard, but she is the opposite of it: her vineyard is her own to give, not bought or for sale.

options.text: She has nothing worth guarding.
options.note: She guards her integrity as something precious, a wall with towers.

quiz.q: Why can love not be bought, according to 8:7?

options.text: Because true love is given, not purchased; wealth offered for it would be scorned.
options.note: Love's worth is beyond price; it can only be freely given and received.

options.text: Because love is cheap and not worth much.
options.note: The opposite: love is beyond all price, so wealth cannot buy it.

options.text: Because the rich are simply too stingy.
options.note: Wealth is truly in view, but the point is the nature of love itself, priceless and freely given, not the stinginess of the wealthy.

options.text: Because only Solomon could afford it.
options.note: Solomon's great wealth is indeed set against love, but precisely to show that love is priceless and not for sale at any price, not that only the rich could buy it.

quiz.q: How does love as strong as death point to the gospel?

options.text: Christ's love went into death and overcame it, unquenchable and freely given, sealing His people as His own.
options.note: At the cross love met death and proved stronger; believers are sealed with the Spirit.

options.text: It teaches that we must earn God's love by our strength.
options.note: Love here is indeed strong, but it cannot be bought or earned by our strength; it is freely given, as Christ gave Himself.

options.text: It shows that death finally defeats love.
options.note: Love is as strong as death and stronger; in Christ death is swallowed up in victory.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ and the church.
options.note: It truly celebrates human love as strong as death, yet the church has long heard here the jealous, unquenchable love of God in Christ, Romans 8:38 to 39, so it does point to the gospel.

questions: Love is as strong as death. How does it steady you to know that the love of Christ went into death itself and came out stronger, so that nothing can separate you from it?
The bride asks to be a seal over her beloved's heart. Have you rested in the truth that Christ holds His people as His own and has sealed you with His Spirit?
Many waters cannot quench love. What floods, of trouble, guilt, or doubt, have felt able to put out God's love for you, and how does this verse answer them?
Love cannot be bought, only given. Where are you tempted to try to earn love, from God or others, that can only be received as a gift?
The bride kept her integrity, her love her own to give. What would it look like to guard and then freely give your love and devotion with that kind of wholeness?

translationNotes.note: A seal, chotam, marked ownership and was worn over the heart or on the arm; jealousy here, with a footnote passion, is fierce, exclusive devotion, not petty envy, the same zeal Scripture ascribes to God.
The fiercest blaze of all renders a Hebrew phrase that many take as a flame of the LORD, hinting that this love's ultimate source is God Himself.
A thousand shekels of silver, literally a thousand of silver, evokes great wealth; Solomon's leased vineyard is set against the bride's own vineyard, her love, which is hers to give and not for sale.
